hero.name: Manish
hero.who: a 40-year-old sales manager in Gurugram whose days vanish into meetings and messages

story.b: Manish leaves his flat in Sector 56 at eight, and by the time his cab reaches the office, he has forty-one unread messages. His calendar is a wall of colour: reviews, client calls, a meeting about the next meeting. He answers emails during lunch and team chats while walking to the washroom. At home he scrolls cricket highlights on the sofa until his eyes ache. His daughter Ira, who is nine, has asked him for three weeks to teach her chess, the game he used to love. Each night he says tomorrow. One Sunday he realises he cannot remember a single thing he did that week that he actually cared about. Every day was full, and none of it was his.

ask.q: Manish's days are packed, yet nothing he cares about gets done. What is the most useful first change?
o: Wake up an hour earlier to fit in more work
Download a better to-do app to track all his tasks
Make daily room for one thing that matters, before the day fills up
ask.why: His problem is not too little effort. Everything urgent crowds out what he values. More hours or a longer task list just feed the same busyness. Choosing room for one thing that matters, before the day starts, puts it ahead of the flood.

chapters.take: A full day is not the same as a day that mattered.

story.b: On Monday night Manish writes one line on a yellow sticky note and sticks it to his laptop: chess with Ira, seven to seven forty-five. Just one thing. He blocks the time in his calendar too, marked busy. On Tuesday the office runs as usual, but every time he opens the laptop, the note is there. At half past five, a colleague asks if they can jump on a quick call at seven. Manish feels the old reflex to say yes. Instead he offers eight fifteen. He reaches home with ten minutes to spare. Ira has already set up the board on the dining table, the wrong way round, and is grinning at him.

ask.q: A colleague asks for a call at seven, right when Manish planned chess with Ira. What should he do?
o: Offer another time and protect the slot he chose for his highlight
Take the call, since work must always come first
Try to do both, playing chess with the phone on speaker
ask.why: A highlight only works if it is protected like any other meeting. Offering a different time usually costs nothing at work. Taking the call teaches him the highlight is optional, and playing chess during a call gives Ira only half a father.

chapters.take: Pick one highlight a day and guard its time like a meeting.

story.b: Manish notices that his evenings still leak away. He sits down for five minutes of cricket highlights after dinner and looks up an hour later. The apps keep refilling with something new. So he makes his phone more boring. He moves the video app off the home screen, logs out of two social apps and switches off every notification except calls and family messages. Now opening a feed means typing a password, and most nights that small hassle is enough to stop him. The first evening he reaches for the phone eight times out of habit. By Friday he is reading a chess book he bought years ago, and he learns a new opening to show Ira.

ask.q: Manish keeps losing evenings to endless highlight videos. Which change will work best?
o: Watch only on weekends but keep the apps on his home screen
Log out and move the apps away so scrolling takes extra effort
Set a daily screen time reminder and try to obey it
ask.why: Endless feeds are built to keep him swimming, so reminders get swept aside when he is tired. A weekend rule with the apps right there is easy to break. Adding friction means distraction takes effort, and his attention stays free for what he chose.

chapters.take: Make distraction a little harder, and focus becomes a little easier.

story.b: Manish looks at his Thursday calendar. Six meetings, back to back. In two of them he mostly listens and nods. He declines one with a polite note asking for the minutes, and changes his weekly team review from sixty minutes to thirty. He also closes his email for the first ninety minutes each morning and finally finishes the quarterly sales plan that has been stuck for weeks. Some people are surprised. His boss, Mr Bhatia, asks why he was offline at ten. Manish shows him the finished plan. Mr Bhatia reads it, nods, and asks him to share the thirty-minute review format with the other managers.

ask.q: Manish's calendar is full of meetings where he only listens. What is the best step?
o: Decline or shorten the ones where he is not needed and protect focus time
Attend all of them, since being busy shows commitment
Attend but quietly answer emails during each one
ask.why: Being busy is not the same as doing useful work. Changing his defaults, like shorter reviews and fewer meetings, gives him time for real progress. Attending everything just feeds the busy habit, and half-listening while emailing wastes both the meeting and his focus.

chapters.take: Busy is a habit, not a goal. Change the defaults that keep you there.

story.b: By three every afternoon, Manish's energy crashes. He usually fixes it with his fourth coffee and a packet of chips from the vending machine. This week he tries something older. After lunch he leaves his phone on the desk and walks ten minutes around the office complex, past the chai stall and the rows of parked bikes. He packs dal, roti and a cucumber from home instead of ordering burgers. He sleeps by eleven, since the phone is boring now anyway. On Saturday he chats with his neighbour over the balcony railing for half an hour. By Thursday the afternoon crash is softer. He still feels tired some days, but he no longer reaches for the chips.

ask.q: Manish crashes every afternoon and his focus disappears. What should he try first?
o: Add another coffee and push through the slump
Try small daily habits like a phone-free walk, real food and better sleep
Skip lunch so he does not feel sleepy afterwards
ask.why: Energy for focus often comes from simple habits like movement, daylight, real food and rest. More coffee only covers the tiredness for a while, and skipping meals can leave him even more drained. If the tiredness never lifts, he should check with a doctor.

chapters.take: Focus runs on energy, and energy comes from moving, eating and sleeping well.

story.b: Every night Manish writes one line in a small notebook beside his bed: what helped today, and what got in the way. After two weeks he reads them back like a scientist reading results. Closing email in the morning works brilliantly. The walk helps. But one tactic keeps failing. He tried waking at five to read, and on four mornings out of five he just lay there, groggy and annoyed. His notes say it plainly. He drops the five o'clock plan and moves reading to the cab ride instead, where he usually just stares at traffic. The new slot works from the very first day. The notebook is slowly turning into a routine that fits his life.

ask.q: Manish's five o'clock wake-up has failed four days out of five. What should he do?
o: Force himself to keep trying until it finally sticks
Give up on all the new tactics, since they clearly do not suit him
Drop that one tactic, keep what works and try a different slot
ask.why: Treating tactics as experiments means keeping what works and dropping what does not. Forcing a failed plan wastes energy and creates guilt. Abandoning everything throws away the tactics that clearly helped. A small change based on his own notes builds a routine that fits him.

chapters.take: Treat every tactic as an experiment. Keep what works, drop the rest.

story.b: Six weeks later, Manish's calendar is still busy, but it no longer runs him. Each night he writes one highlight on a sticky note. Some days it is a client pitch, some days it is cooking rajma for the family, and on Tuesdays and Fridays it is chess with Ira. His team now holds thirty-minute reviews, and two other managers have copied the format. The video apps are still logged out. He reads on the cab ride and walks after lunch. Last Tuesday Ira beat him in eleven moves and ran around the flat cheering. Manish laughed so hard he did not even notice that his phone, face down on the shelf, had buzzed four times.

chapters.take: Making time is not about doing more. It is about choosing what to remember.
